Based on these findings, the paper recommends that pediatricians and endocrinologists critically assess the care offered to adolescents and young adults, adopt new approaches to help improve glycemic control during the vulnerable late-teen years, optimize transition strategies to adult care, and strictly adhere to clinical guidelines regarding blood pressure and kidney protection medications for patients with nephropathy.

Over the 10-year period, adjusted mean HbA1c significantly improved from 68 mmol/mol (8.4%) to 63 mmol/mol (7.9%), coinciding with an increase in insulin pump use from 25.7% to 41.8% and continuous glucose monitoring sensor use from 1.5% to 44.6%. The percentage of patients achieving the target HbA1c of <7% (<53 mmol/mol) rose from 21% in 2008 to 34% in 2018, while severe hypoglycemia rates dropped from 3.8% to 2.4%, and secondary cardiovascular risk factors such as BMI-standard deviation score improved. The findings suggest that twice-yearly international benchmarking, standardized quality control, continuous data monitoring, and the adoption of modern diabetes technologies within centers of reference are effective strategies for improving long-term metabolic outcomes in pediatric type 1 diabetes care.
passage_2: The Hvidoere Childhood Diabetes Study Group Centre Differences Study 2005 evaluates the glycaemic targets set by diabetes teams, how these targets are perceived by adolescents with type 1 diabetes and their parents, and their overall influence on metabolic control across 21 international centres. In an assessment of 2,062 adolescents, the study found a mean HbA1c of 8.2%, with significant variation between centres ranging from 7.4% to 9.1%. Key findings revealed a significant positive correlation between the HbA1c levels that adolescents and parents reported they would be happy with—as well as their perceived ideal targets—and their actual HbA1c results, with lower target HbA1c setting and greater consistency among multidisciplinary team members directly associating with lower overall centre HbA1c levels. Ultimately, the paper concludes that target setting plays a significant role in driving the metabolic differences observed across centres, demonstrating that clear and consistent setting of glycaemic targets by pediatric diabetes teams strongly improves HbA1c outcomes.

Over the 10-year period, adjusted mean HbA1c significantly improved from 68 mmol/mol (8.4%) to 63 mmol/mol (7.9%), coinciding with an increase in insulin pump use from 25.7% to 41.8% and continuous glucose monitoring sensor use from 1.5% to 44.6%. It finds that type 1 diabetes is characterized by autoimmune beta-cell destruction leading to lifelong insulin dependence, affecting millions globally with substantial age-related and geographic variation in incidence. The study recommends recognizing clinical presentation variations between youth and adults, utilizing pancreatic autoantibody panels to differentiate type 1 from type 2 diabetes, and establishing early, structured transition plans from pediatric to adult clinical care teams. Additionally, guidelines provided in the paper outline standardized diagnostic criteria—such as fasting plasma glucose and A1C thresholds—alongside scheduled protocols for initial, quarterly, and annual evaluations covering microvascular and macrovascular complication screenings, autoimmune comorbidity checks, and individualized self-management support across all developmental stages.
passage_2: The study Glycemic control and complications in patients with type 1 diabetes – a registry-based longitudinal study of adolescents and young adults evaluates longitudinal glycemic control, the prevalence of microvascular complications (retinopathy and nephropathy), and the impact of transition timing from pediatric to adult care among 874 young people with type 1 diabetes in Norway using data linked from two nationwide registries. Findings demonstrate that youth-onset type 2 diabetes is characterized by severe insulin resistance and a rapid decline in pancreatic β-cell function that progresses three to four times faster than in adults, leading to significantly higher therapeutic failure rates with standard metformin treatment. The disease disproportionately affects minority racial and ethnic groups as well as female adolescents, with rising pediatric obesity clouding the clinical distinction between obese type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes. To address this growing health crisis, the authors highlight guidelines and recommendations for urgent development of novel, approved pharmacotherapeutic agents that target pediatric pathophysiological mechanisms alongside aggressive lifestyle and community-based prevention initiatives to halt the projected fourfold increase in youth type 2 diabetes by 2050.

The findings suggest that twice-yearly international benchmarking, standardized quality control, continuous data monitoring, and the adoption of modern diabetes technologies within centers of reference are effective strategies for improving long-term metabolic outcomes in pediatric type 1 diabetes care.

It finds that type 1 diabetes is characterized by autoimmune beta-cell destruction leading to lifelong insulin dependence, affecting millions globally with substantial age-related and geographic variation in incidence. The study recommends recognizing clinical presentation variations between youth and adults, utilizing pancreatic autoantibody panels to differentiate type 1 from type 2 diabetes, and establishing early, structured transition plans from pediatric to adult clinical care teams. Additionally, guidelines provided in the paper outline standardized diagnostic criteria—such as fasting plasma glucose and A1C thresholds—alongside scheduled protocols for initial, quarterly, and annual evaluations covering microvascular and macrovascular complication screenings, autoimmune comorbidity checks, and individualized self-management support across all developmental stages.
passage_2: The study Glycemic control and complications in patients with type 1 diabetes – a registry-based longitudinal study of adolescents and young adults evaluates longitudinal glycemic control, the prevalence of microvascular complications (retinopathy and nephropathy), and the impact of transition timing from pediatric to adult care among 874 young people with type 1 diabetes in Norway using data linked from two nationwide registries. Additionally, patients who transferred to adult care before age 18 had significantly higher HbA1c levels and a higher prevalence of complications than those who transferred between ages 18–22, while less than 40% of patients with albuminuria were receiving recommended ACE inhibitor or ARB treatment. Based on these findings, the paper recommends that pediatricians and endocrinologists critically assess the care offered to adolescents and young adults, adopt new approaches to help improve glycemic control during the vulnerable late-teen years, optimize transition strategies to adult care, and strictly adhere to clinical guidelines regarding blood pressure and kidney protection medications for patients with nephropathy.

The percentage of patients achieving the target HbA1c of <7% (<53 mmol/mol) rose from 21% in 2008 to 34% in 2018, while severe hypoglycemia rates dropped from 3.8% to 2.4%, and secondary cardiovascular risk factors such as BMI-standard deviation score improved. In an assessment of 2,062 adolescents, the study found a mean HbA1c of 8.2%, with significant variation between centres ranging from 7.4% to 9.1%. Key findings revealed a significant positive correlation between the HbA1c levels that adolescents and parents reported they would be happy with—as well as their perceived ideal targets—and their actual HbA1c results, with lower target HbA1c setting and greater consistency among multidisciplinary team members directly associating with lower overall centre HbA1c levels. Ultimately, the paper concludes that target setting plays a significant role in driving the metabolic differences observed across centres, demonstrating that clear and consistent setting of glycaemic targets by pediatric diabetes teams strongly improves HbA1c outcomes.
passage_2: The study Decision-Making Involvement and Prediction of Adherence in Youth With Type 1 Diabetes: A Cohort Sequential Study evaluates developmental trajectories of decision-making involvement (DMI)—defined as the ways in which parents and children engage each other regarding T1D management—and examines how DMI impacts adherence levels and age-related changes over time in youth aged 8 to 16 assessed five times over two years. Findings revealed that most DMI aspects increased with age, though certain child-reported subscales (Parent Express, Child Seek, and Joint) peaked around ages 12–14 before declining; additionally, higher levels of Child Seek, Child Express, and Joint behaviors were significantly associated with higher overall treatment adherence in both parent and youth reports, though DMI did not significantly alter the rate of adherence decline over time. Recommendations and guidelines suggest targeting interventions toward encouraging proactive child participation in T1D discussions—specifically coaching youth to share information, express opinions, and solicit parental guidance—to support effective self-management as children transition toward greater autonomy.

passage_1: The study Glycemic control and complications in patients with type 1 diabetes – a registry-based longitudinal study of adolescents and young adults evaluates longitudinal glycemic control, the prevalence of microvascular complications (retinopathy and nephropathy), and the impact of transition timing from pediatric to adult care among 874 young people with type 1 diabetes in Norway using data linked from two nationwide registries. Microvascular complications were prevalent, with 16% of participants exhibiting retinopathy and 13% exhibiting nephropathy; higher HbA1c levels across adolescence and young adulthood, longer diabetes duration, younger age at diagnosis, and smoking were strongly associated with a higher risk of complications. Additionally, patients who transferred to adult care before age 18 had significantly higher HbA1c levels and a higher prevalence of complications than those who transferred between ages 18–22, while less than 40% of patients with albuminuria were receiving recommended ACE inhibitor or ARB treatment. Based on these findings, the paper recommends that pediatricians and endocrinologists critically assess the care offered to adolescents and young adults, adopt new approaches to help improve glycemic control during the vulnerable late-teen years, optimize transition strategies to adult care, and strictly adhere to clinical guidelines regarding blood pressure and kidney protection medications for patients with nephropathy.
passage_2: The study titled Type 1 Diabetes Through the Life Span: A Position Statement of the American Diabetes Association evaluates the global and domestic incidence, diagnostic challenges, and comprehensive management strategies for type 1 diabetes across all age groups. It finds that type 1 diabetes is characterized by autoimmune beta-cell destruction leading to lifelong insulin dependence, affecting millions globally with substantial age-related and geographic variation in incidence. The study recommends recognizing clinical presentation variations between youth and adults, utilizing pancreatic autoantibody panels to differentiate type 1 from type 2 diabetes, and establishing early, structured transition plans from pediatric to adult clinical care teams. Additionally, guidelines provided in the paper outline standardized diagnostic criteria—such as fasting plasma glucose and A1C thresholds—alongside scheduled protocols for initial, quarterly, and annual evaluations covering microvascular and macrovascular complication screenings, autoimmune comorbidity checks, and individualized self-management support across all developmental stages.

Additionally, non-fasting HbA1c screening is more practical, reproducible, and has been shown to increase diabetes screening rates and early detection among adolescents. The paper recommends that American Diabetes Association (ADA) diagnostic criteria remain useful for screening at-risk, asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic pediatric populations, with laboratory-based HbA1c certified by the National Glycohemoglobin Standardization Program (NGSP) being the preferred method; practitioners should exercise clinical judgment when diagnostic test results conflict, and HbA1c should be avoided in cases of pregnancy, cystic fibrosis, or hemoglobinopathies and disorders causing high red blood cell turnover.

The study found that while 25.5% of US youth met screening criteria, the sensitivity and specificity of these criteria were low for detecting hyperglycemia. Confirmed undiagnosed diabetes was rare (less than 0.5% of youth), with over 85% of diabetes cases already diagnosed. Furthermore, HbA1c-defined hyperglycemia showed significantly stronger and more specific associations with cardiometabolic risk compared to FPG-defined hyperglycemia. Based on these findings, the study highlights HbA1c as a highly specific, effective nonfasting test to identify high-risk youth who could benefit from lifestyle interventions to prevent diabetes and cardiovascular risks later in life.

Alongside these glycemic gains, the uptake of diabetes technology increased significantly across continuous glucose monitors, insulin pumps, and hybrid closed-loop systems; however, pronounced health inequities persisted, as non-Hispanic White and privately insured individuals consistently maintained better glycemic outcomes and higher device adoption rates than non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, and publicly insured patients. Based on these insights, the study highlights the need for targeted quality improvement interventions, policy adjustments, and funded research to directly address socio-behavioral barriers and ensure equitable access to diabetes technology and care across diverse populations.
passage_2: The SWEET Project 10-Year Benchmarking study evaluates time trends of key quality indicators and the impact of treatment changes in 16,082 youth with type 1 diabetes across 22 centers in 19 countries between 2008–2010 and 2016–2018. Over the 10-year period, adjusted mean HbA1c significantly improved from 68 mmol/mol (8.4%) to 63 mmol/mol (7.9%), coinciding with an increase in insulin pump use from 25.7% to 41.8% and continuous glucose monitoring sensor use from 1.5% to 44.6%. The percentage of patients achieving the target HbA1c of <7% (<53 mmol/mol) rose from 21% in 2008 to 34% in 2018, while severe hypoglycemia rates dropped from 3.8% to 2.4%, and secondary cardiovascular risk factors such as BMI-standard deviation score improved. The findings suggest that twice-yearly international benchmarking, standardized quality control, continuous data monitoring, and the adoption of modern diabetes technologies within centers of reference are effective strategies for improving long-term metabolic outcomes in pediatric type 1 diabetes care.

Between 2013 and 2022, aggregate mean HbA1c dropped from 8.2% to 7.6%, and the proportion of children reaching an HbA1c target below 7% increased from 19.0% to 38.8%, alongside marked increases in insulin pump usage (42.9% to 60.2%) and continuous glucose monitoring uptake (18.7% in 2016 to 81.7% in 2022). Based on these results, the paper recommends that future shared decision-making trials seek to actively promote decision aid engagement—particularly among non-White adolescents, potentially via direct assistance during the initial login—and explicitly guidelines that trials employing electronic decision aids routinely measure, report, and analyze objective utilization data.
passage_2: The study "Systematic Review: Diabetes Family Conflict in Young People With Type 1 Diabetes" evaluates the relationships between diabetes-specific family conflict and various health outcomes—including glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), treatment adherence, blood glucose monitoring, depression, anxiety, quality of life, and well-being—among young people with type 1 diabetes aged 14 to 25 years. Across 20 included studies, greater diabetes-specific family conflict was significantly associated with higher HbA1c values in 17 studies, suboptimal treatment adherence or less frequent blood glucose monitoring in 7 studies, and poorer quality of life, reduced well-being, or heightened depressive and anxiety symptoms in 7 studies, though 4 studies found no significant links to HbA1c or adherence. Given these findings, the authors recommend routine screening for and intervention addressing diabetes-specific family conflict in clinical practice, while highlighting guidelines for future research to prioritize longitudinal studies specifically targeting young people over the age of 16.

passage_1: Evidence-Based Behavioral Interventions to Promote Diabetes Management in Children, Adolescents, and Families evaluates contemporary psychological and behavioral interventions designed to support self-management, adherence, and health outcomes among youth with type 1 diabetes (T1D) and type 2 diabetes (T2D) and their families within key theoretical frameworks like Social Cognitive Theory, Family Systems Theory, and Social Ecological Models. Findings demonstrate that structured behavioral approaches—such as skills training, family-based teamwork, behavioral family systems therapy, and multi-systemic therapies—yield modest yet clinically meaningful improvements in regimen adherence, quality of life, and glycemic control, particularly when delivered early post-diagnosis, incorporating family collaboration, or targeting modifiable emotional and family processes rather than relying solely on education. Recommendations highlight tailoring behavioral interventions to meet the unique strengths and needs of individual families, evaluating cost-effectiveness for broader translation, combining mobile and digital health technologies with human contact, and conducting further culturally tailored research for youth with T2D. Finally, guidelines set by national and international diabetes organizations call for routine psychological screening and referral to evidence-based mental health therapies as standard components of pediatric clinical diabetes care.
passage_2: The paper, "Contemporary Roles of the Pediatric Psychologist in Diabetes Care," evaluates the diverse clinical, administrative, and research roles that pediatric psychologists play in managing diabetes among children and adolescents across various treatment phases—including diagnosis, outpatient visits, and inpatient hospitalizations—and settings such as academic medical centers, private practice, and community organizations. Findings highlight that major healthcare organizations recognize psychologists as essential members of the interdisciplinary diabetes care team, contributing through screening, individual, family, and group interventions, as well as translational research and program development for youth transitioning to adult care. The authors recommend embedding pediatric psychologists directly into integrated diabetes clinics to deliver comprehensive medical and psychosocial care in a single visit, alongside increasing advocacy to expand clinical engagement, billing models, and translational research opportunities in pediatric diabetes management.
passage_3: Codesigned Shared Decision-Making Diabetes Management Plan Tool for Adolescents With Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus and Their Parents: Prototype Development and Pilot Test evaluates the process of codesigning a clinic-based shared decision-making diabetes management plan tool alongside a patient and parent advisory board (PAB) consisting of six adolescents with type 1 diabetes mellitus and their parents. The study found six key quality-of-life measurement domains affecting families—stress, fear and worry, mealtime struggles, assumptions and judgments, feeling abnormal, and conflict—and highlighted that adolescents prioritize social inclusion and reducing family conflict over traditional clinical health outcomes. Based on these findings, the paper recommends utilizing shared decision-making tools in clinical encounters that focus directly on diabetes distress, conflict resolution strategies, and establishing mutually verbalized common goals rather than imposing authoritarian behavioral contracts.
